claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: MASA achieves consistent accuracy gains across multiple sparse methods, benchmarks, and backbones
claims.claim_text_verbatim: Extensive experiments across multiple sparse attention methods, benchmarks, and LLM backbones show consistent accuracy gains, supporting both MASA and the matrix-approximation view of sparse attention.

evidence_spans.source_text: MASA improves all eight matched average scores across three sparse methods, three benchmark suites, and both Llama- and Qwen-family backbones.
Within each framework, Original and MASA use the same LLM backbone, benchmark, candidate units, sparse kernel, and sparse budget, differing only in the ranking score.

claims.claim_summary: MASA's accuracy gains are larger at 32K–128K contexts than at 4K–16K contexts
claims.claim_text_verbatim: For every configuration, the mean gain over these longer contexts at 32K–128K exceeds that at 4K–16K.

evidence_spans.source_text: At 128K, MASA improves MInference, SeerAttention, FlexPrefill-Llama, and FlexPrefill-Qwen by 1.28, 0.48, 1.45, and 2.16 points, respectively. At 64K, the gains reach 2.16 points for FlexPrefill-Llama and 3.65 points for FlexPrefill-Qwen.

claims.claim_summary: MASA significantly reduces attention-output approximation error across all tested model frameworks
claims.claim_text_verbatim: Table 8 shows lower attention-output error in every evaluated framework–backbone pair, with all four reported paired confidence intervals above zero.

evidence_spans.source_text: Table 8: Attention-output error decreases across all four evaluated framework–backbone pairs. Original and MASA denote the baseline and diagnostic configuration. E is the normalized squared output error in Eq. (27). Relative reductions and paired 98.75% confidence intervals are reported in percent. Bold marks the lower error and the positive reduction.
The relative reductions are 0.41% for MInference, 2.10% for SeerAttention, and 2.34% and 7.17% for FlexPrefill on Llama and Qwen, respectively.
